passage: The school gates opened at 7:45, and Ishita's car always pulled up at 7:40, cool air still on her arms. Today she noticed Pranav coming through the side gate, shirt stuck to his back, shoes grey with dust. "Where do you live?" she asked at the water cooler. "Past the brick kiln. Four kilometres. I walk with my sister." "Every day? Why don't you take a bus?" Pranav shrugged. "No bus goes there." In class, Ishita kept looking at his dusty shoes. Four kilometres. She felt something prickly, a bit like being caught cheating, though she hadn't done anything. At lunch she asked Ms D'Costa, "Why doesn't the bus go to Pranav's side?" Ms D'Costa put down her tiffin. "That's a very good question, Ishita. Let's find out together."

qa.q: How far does Pranav walk to school?
qa.a: Four kilometres, from past the brick kiln.

qa.q: What was the prickly feeling Ishita had in class?
qa.a: It was a kind of guilt, "like being caught cheating", though she hadn't done anything wrong.

qa.q: Ishita chose to ask Ms D'Costa why the bus doesn't go there. Why is that a good next step?
qa.a: It turns her guilty feeling into curiosity about the reason, and an adult can help her understand it instead of her just feeling bad.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt being asked "Why don't you take a bus?"
qa.a: Pranav may have felt a bit awkward explaining, since the answer, no bus goes there, is something he can't change.

grounding: A child who arrives by car notices a classmate walks four kilometres to school, feels uneasy, and starts asking why.

passage: I'm Rukmini, Kamal's didi. Last week Kamal's friend Sonu came over to do homework, and I watched something change in my little brother. Sonu stared at Kamal's desk and lamp for a long time. "You have your own table?" At Sonu's house, he said, there's one room and the TV is always on, so he does sums on the steps outside. Kamal went quiet. After Sonu left, Kamal asked Amma, "Why does Sonu's house only have one room?" Amma tried to explain about rent and jobs. Then I teased, "See, you're lucky," and Kamal got cross. "I didn't do anything wrong!" He stomped off. But that night I saw him clearing half his desk and asking Amma if Sonu could come every Tuesday. I don't know exactly what he was feeling. Something big, for nine.

qa.q: Where does Sonu do his sums at home?
qa.a: On the steps outside, because the TV is always on in the one room.

qa.q: Why might Kamal have got cross when Rukmini said "you're lucky"?
qa.a: He seemed to feel accused, as if having a desk were his fault, so he defended himself: "I didn't do anything wrong!"

qa.q: What did Kamal choose to do that night, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He cleared half his desk and asked if Sonu could come every Tuesday, turning his discomfort into a way to share 🙂

qa.q: How might Sonu feel coming over on Tuesdays?
qa.a: Sonu might enjoy a quiet table for sums and feel welcome, as long as it's offered as friendship rather than pity.

grounding: An older sister watches her little brother notice his friend has no quiet place to study, ask why, get defensive, and then share.

passage:
Monday. Divyansh got 18 out of 20 in the maths test and grinned. Mohit got 17. "I go to tuition three days a week," Divyansh told him. "Don't you?" Mohit shook his head.
Thursday. Buying pencils at the market, Divyansh saw Mohit behind the counter of his father's tea stall, doing homework between customers, the book balanced on a crate. Mohit waved. Divyansh waved back, then felt oddly hot. "Well, I study hard too," he muttered to his mother, though nobody had said he didn't.
Next Monday. At dinner Divyansh asked, "Papa, why does Mohit have to work at the shop?" Papa thought for a while before answering. The next day Divyansh brought his old guidebooks to school and slid them onto Mohit's desk. "I finished these. Want them?"

qa.q: What score did Mohit get in the maths test?
qa.a: Mohit got 17.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh mutter "I study hard too" when nobody had said otherwise?
qa.a: Seeing Mohit working at the stall made him uncomfortable, maybe a little guilty, so he became defensive.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Divyansh, and what did he do with it?
qa.a: Asking Papa why Mohit has to work was the turning point; the next day he offered Mohit his old guidebooks.

qa.q: How might Mohit have taken Divyansh's question about tuition on Monday?
qa.a: Mohit may have felt a little small, since tuition isn't an option for him and his 17 came without it.

grounding: Over a week a child notices a classmate studies at his father's stall without tuition, feels defensive, asks why, and shares.

passage: Neelam, you asked why I keep an extra lamp by the door. Listen to your Charu Nani. When I was nine, the power went every evening in our town. Our house had a generator, so I did homework under a bright bulb. One night I walked to the shop with Papa and saw my friend Shabnam sitting under the streetlight by the post office, copying sums and squinting. Next day I asked Amma, "Why does Shabnam study outside?" Amma said their house had no generator. My face went hot. I even said, "It's not my fault!" though nobody had said it was. But after that I kept asking why. Some evenings Shabnam came over, and we shared my bulb.

qa.q: Where was Shabnam studying?
qa.a: Under the streetlight by the post office, copying sums.

qa.q: Why did Charu burst out with "It's not my fault!" when nobody had blamed anyone?
qa.a: Charu felt guilty and a bit defensive on seeing the difference, so the words came out as if pushing blame away.

qa.q: What choice did young Charu make after that hot-faced moment, and what did it change?
qa.a: Charu kept asking why and invited Shabnam over to share the bright bulb, turning an uncomfortable feeling into something useful.

qa.q: What might those evenings under the streetlight have been like for Shabnam?
qa.a: Shabnam was probably used to squinting and just getting the sums done; sharing the bulb may have felt kind, as long as it came as friendship and not pity.

grounding: A child notices that a friend studies under a streetlight while their own home has light, feels guilty and defensive, and starts to ask why.

passage: The rain came down so hard that the headmistress sent everyone home at noon. Kishore climbed into the yellow school van, dry under his raincoat. Through the steamy window he saw Dolma tie a plastic bag over her books and start up the steep path behind the school, alone. "Uncle, why doesn't the van go to Dolma's side?" "No road there, only steps. Forty minutes' walk." Forty minutes. Kishore got home in five. He felt strange, as if he'd taken something without asking. Next morning he asked Dolma, "Do you walk every day? Even in exams?" "Every day," she said, shrugging. "I learn my spellings on the steps." That night Kishore asked his mother why some roads just stop.

qa.q: How long is Dolma's walk home?
qa.a: Forty minutes' walk, up steps.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling after he got home dry?
qa.a: He felt strange and a little guilty, as if he'd taken something without asking, because his ride was so much easier than Dolma's walk.

qa.q: What did Kishore do with that uneasy feeling, and why was it a good choice?
qa.a: He asked questions, first Dolma and then his mother, instead of looking away, which is how he started to understand that some children begin further back.

qa.q: How might Dolma see the walk, compared with how Kishore sees it?
qa.a: For Dolma it is simply every day, and she even uses it to learn spellings, while to Kishore it suddenly looks long and unfair 🤔

grounding: A child driven home in the rain sees a classmate climb a long path alone and starts asking why their starting points are so different.
